The Victorian Era. The reign of Queen Victoria of Britain, spanning 64 years from 1837 to 1901 of unprecedented industrial, economic, and imperial expansion. The period witnessed Britain's ascendancy as the world's dominant industrial and military power, moral debates over propriety and progress, literary and artistic flourishing, and deep social anxieties over modernization, class, and the empire's moral foundations.

Queen Victoria's accession in 1837 initiated an era of conservative moralism and emphasis on duty, propriety, and family values. Victorianism became synonymous with sexual restraint and social hierarchy. The Industrial Revolution reached its apex during Victoria's reign. Steam power, railways, factories, and urban growth transformed Britain from agrarian to industrial, creating unprecedented wealth and dislocation.

Britain became the world's premier imperial power, controlling India, vast African territories, Australia, and dominions. The Raj represented both industrial organization and racial hierarchy, glorified at home but destabilizing abroad. The Great Exhibition in 1851 showcased British industrial achievement and was the most visited event of the era. It symbolized confidence in progress, technology, and British superiority.

Class tensions mounted as industrialization created a powerful industrial bourgeoisie, a growing working class, and a destabilized landed aristocracy. Political reform expanded the franchise in 1867 and 1884, gradually democratizing the political system. Literature flourished. Charles Dickens, George Eliot, Thomas Hardy, Oscar Wilde, and George Bernard Shaw created masterpieces grappling with modernization, morality, hypocrisy, and social injustice.

The era's end was marked by anxiety. The Boer War from 1899 to 1902 shattered assumptions of British invincibility. The death of Victoria in 1901 closed a psychological epoch.
